title: Basset Hound
wiki_lead:
The Basset Hound is a short-legged breed of scent hound. The Basset Hound was developed in Great Britain from several now-extinct strains of French basset breeds. It was bred primarily for hunting rabbit and hare on foot, moving slowly enough that horses were not required. Their sense of smell and ability to ground-scent is second only to the Bloodhound.
Basset Hounds are one of six recognized "basset"-type breeds in France. The name Basset is derived from the French word bas, meaning 'low', with the attenuating suffix -et—together meaning 'rather low'. Basset Hounds are usually bicolours or tricolours of standard hound coloration.

The Basset Hound is a short-legged breed of scent hound. The Basset Hound was developed in Great Britain from several now-extinct strains of French basset breeds. It was bred primarily for hunting rabbit and hare on foot, moving slowly enough that horses were not required. Their sense of smell and ability to ground-scent is second only to the Bloodhound.
Basset Hounds are one of six recognized "basset"-type breeds in France. The name Basset is derived from the French word bas, meaning 'low', with the attenuating suffix -et—together meaning 'rather low'. Basset Hounds are usually bicolours or tricolours of standard hound coloration.


Description


Appearance
Basset Hounds are proportionally akin to a large breed dog with short legs. Their slightly-curved tail is held high above their long backs. Size and weight is variable between bloodlines, but weigh between 20 and 35 kg (44 and 77 pounds) on average. This breed, relative to size, is heavier-boned than any other breed.
Similar to the bloodhound, the Basset Hound has wrinkled, loose skin that incites a sad expression. The loose skin around the neck is known as the dewlap. The characteristic long ears help to stir up ground scent. They have slightly crook'd legs that help to support the broad chest and ribs.
The coat is most-often short with coarse hairs under the tail. They come in all hound colors except merle and brindle. The most popular colors tend to be variations in tricolor patterns, but they also come in various shades of red and white.


Temperament

The Basset Hound is a friendly, outgoing, and playful dog, tolerant of children and other pets. Their temperament is typically mild and extremely devoted, though not timid.


Health


Osteochondrodysplasia
The Basset Hound's short stature is due to the genetic condition osteochondrodysplasia. Osteochondrodysplasia causes stunted growth and impacts movement. Affected dogs develop splayed hind limbs, enlarged joints, flattened rib cages, shortened and bent long bones, and deformed paws.


Life expectancy
The breed has a median life span of 10–12 years. A 2015 French study found a life expectancy of 10.3 years. A 2024 study in the UK found a life expectancy of 12.5 years compared to an average of 12.7 for purebreeds and 12 for crossbreeds.


Other health issues

Basset Hounds are prone to yeast infections.
Leading causes of death in a 2004 UK Kennel Club survey were cancer (31%), old age (13%), gastric dilatation volvulus (11%), and cardiac (8%).
Information from veterinary data found the prevalence of glaucoma to be 5.44%, second highest in the study.
The Basset Hound is predisposed to gastric dilatation volvulus. One study found the odds ratio to be 5.9.
Basset Hound hereditary thrombopathy is an autosomally inherited platelet disorder characterised by a thrombasthenia defect in primary aggregation abnormality of clot retraction. Glycoprotein IIb-IIIa is defective although detectable.

grok_lead: The Basset Hound is a short-legged breed of scent hound renowned for its exceptional olfactory abilities, second only to the Bloodhound, and its distinctive appearance characterized by long, drooping ears, soulful eyes, and a wrinkled forehead. Originating from France and Belgium, where "basset" derives from the French word for "low," the breed was developed primarily for hunting small game such as rabbits over rough terrain, relying on its powerful nose rather than speed. Typically standing 14 to 15 inches tall at the shoulder and weighing 40 to 65 pounds, Basset Hounds possess a sturdy, heavy-boned frame with massive paws, a smooth, short coat in colors like black and tan, lemon and white, or red and white, and a lifespan of 12 to 13 years. The breed's history traces back to the 6th or 7th century at the Abbey of St. Hubert in the Ardennes region of France, where monks selectively bred short-legged hounds from larger ancestors like the St. Hubert Hound to track game close to the ground. By the 16th century, references to Bassets appear in literature, including Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, and the modern form, featuring achondroplastic dwarfism for a low stature, emerged between the 16th and 19th centuries. First introduced to England in 1866, when Lord Galway received a pair from the Comte de Tournon, and further popularized by figures like Sir Everett Millais using dogs from the Comte le Couteulx de Canteleu, the breed gained recognition from the English Kennel Club in 1880; it arrived in the United States shortly after in 1883, with the American Kennel Club granting official recognition in 1885. The Basset Hound Club of America, founded in 1933, has since worked to preserve the breed's standards and promote its welfare. In temperament, Basset Hounds are gentle, affectionate, and patient companions, often described as "noble clowns" for their laid-back demeanor at home contrasted with their determined stubbornness during hunts. They are generally good with children and other pets due to their mild nature but require consistent training to manage their vocal tendencies and tendency to follow scents independently. As a hound group member, the breed excels in trailing but adapts well to family life with moderate daily exercise, such as walks, though they are prone to health issues like ear infections, obesity, and hip dysplasia, necessitating regular veterinary care.
